analysis.one_liner: Restores employer liability for harassment by supervisors who direct workers' daily jobs, undoing a Supreme Court ruling.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have made employers legally responsible for harassment by anyone with power over a worker's daily job, never received a hearing or a vote and died in committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have reversed the effect of the Supreme Court's 2013 Vance v. Ball State University decision, which limits an employer's legal responsibility for workplace harassment to harassers who have the power to hire and fire. Under this bill, an employer would also be liable when the harasser directs the worker's daily work activities, or when the employer's own negligence allowed a hostile work environment to continue. It would apply across the major federal anti-discrimination laws, including protections based on sex, race, age, disability, and genetics, and would cover private-sector workers, federal employees, and Congressional employees.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who are harassed by shift leads, crew chiefs, or senior co-workers who control their schedules and assignments but cannot formally hire or fire them. The bill's findings point especially to low-wage workers in restaurants, retail, health care, housekeeping, and personal care, where such power-without-title arrangements are common, and to women and people of color who file most harassment charges. Federal employees and Congressional staff would gain the same standard under the Civil Rights Act provisions and the Congressional Accountability Act.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Harassed workers, especially in low-wage service jobs

how_it_helps.text: Restores the pre-2013 definition of a supervisor so employers are legally liable for harassment by anyone authorized to direct an employee's daily work activities, not just those who can take formal hiring and firing actions, under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act and related statutes.

Adds an employer-negligence trigger: employers are liable when their own carelessness allowed a hostile work environment to be created or continue, including for retaliatory hostile work environments.

Extends the same standard to the Age Discrimination in Employment Act, the Americans with Disabilities Act, the Rehabilitation Act, section 1981 race claims, the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act, federal-employee protections, and the Congressional Accountability Act covering Congressional staff.

The bill's own findings document why: women and people of color in low-wage jobs are especially vulnerable, two-thirds of women restaurant workers surveyed reported sexual harassment from management, and workers in retail, restaurants, health care, and housekeeping commonly face harassers who direct their day-to-day work but lack formal hiring power.

analysis.who_pays: Employers — particularly those in industries with high harassment rates, like restaurants, retail, and health care — would bear more liability in lawsuits, larger settlement and judgment exposure, and the cost of stronger prevention and supervision. The bill applies to all claims pending on or after enactment, so some employers with cases already in court would face the new standard.

drawbacks.text: Expanding who counts as a supervisor increases employers' exposure to lawsuits and settlements, including for harassers the employer did not know about, which raises compliance costs that small businesses in thin-margin industries would feel most.
Section 14 makes the new liability standard apply to all claims pending on or after enactment, so businesses with harassment cases already in court would face the changed rules midstream.

The bill preserves the Faragher/Ellerth defenses (an employer's reasonable prevention efforts and a worker's failure to use them) by stating nothing limits available defenses, so the practical gain in any given case depends on how courts weigh those defenses.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the gain is real: the Vance decision narrowed who counts as a supervisor to those with hiring-and-firing power, leaving many low-wage workers with no employer liability claim against the shift leads and crew bosses who actually control their working lives. The cost falls on employers in the form of greater litigation and settlement exposure, and the bill's pending-claims application adds retroactivity concerns. On balance the bill is a straightforward restoration of a liability standard that existed before 2013, aimed at the workers most exposed to harassment, with a modest and defensible cost to employers — but it never got a hearing, so it was never tested or refined.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate committee that handles labor law, which never gave it a hearing or a vote, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Tammy Baldwin introduced the bill on July 25, 2019, joined by Senator Patrick Leahy, to overturn the Supreme Court's Vance v. Ball State University limitation on employer harassment liability.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action was ever taken: the committee held no hearing or markup, the full Senate never voted, and the bill expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
Only one Senate colleague cosponsored the bill, and the committee that controlled its fate was chaired by the opposing party, so the bill never came close to floor consideration.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers — especially in low-wage, high-harassment industries — are better off, because the narrower Vance v. Ball State liability standard they benefit from remains in force and many harassment claims against day-to-day supervisors still fail as a result.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers shielded by the Vance ruling

for.name: Tammy Baldwin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fair Employment Protection Act of 2019 to restore employer liability for harassment by supervisors who direct daily work.

for.name: Patrick Leahy
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; the only other Senate supporter.

against.name: Lamar Alexander
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: The committee of jurisdiction never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill received no action after referral for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill's only supporters were two Senate Democrats, and the Republican-chaired committee that received it took no action, so the partisan shape can only be inferred.

industries.note: The bill's findings cite a survey finding two-thirds of women restaurant workers experienced sexual harassment from management; these employers would face liability for harassers who direct daily work but cannot hire or fire, directly cutting against their interest in limiting such claims.

industries.industry: Retail, health care, housekeeping, and personal care employers
industries.note: The bill identifies these low-wage industries as places where supervisors commonly direct workers' day-to-day activities without formal hiring power; under the bill, employers there would be liable for harassment by those individuals instead of the workers bearing it alone.

industries.industry: Federal agencies and Congressional employing offices
industries.note: The bill extends the broader liability standard to federal executive-branch workplaces, the Smithsonian, and offices covered by the Congressional Accountability Act, meaning government employers could be sued for harassment by day-to-day supervisors.
